Misunderstood Signals in Couples Therapy Online

When Online Couples Therapy Signals Get Crossed

Online couples therapy can make it much easier to get support when life is full. For many Brisbane couples, it means you can talk with a therapist from home, even if one of you works FIFO, travels often, or lives in another city. It can be a relief to log in after work, stay warm inside, and finally talk about things you have been putting off.

At the same time, the screen can change how messages land. Tone can feel sharper, silences can feel heavier, and it can be harder to read each other clearly. Small misunderstandings can grow quickly when they pass through a camera, microphone, and internet connection.

At Michelle Barratt Psychology, we offer evidence-based support for couples in person and through telehealth. We see how easily signals can get crossed online, and we work gently and clearly to help partners notice, name, and repair those moments before they turn into bigger fights or quiet distance.

How Misunderstandings Multiply Through a Screen

Online sessions can be very helpful, but the tech itself can create a few traps. When you are already feeling tense, these small issues can feel very personal.

Common tech problems can include:

  • Delays in sound, so answers feel slow or off-topic
  • Glitches or frozen screens, so faces look blank or stuck
  • Echoes or poor audio, so words are hard to hear

If one partner shares something important and the other person pauses because the sound cut out, that pause might look like disinterest. When the screen freezes on a neutral face, it might be read as a cold stare. What is really a Wi-Fi problem can feel like rejection.

Body language can also be harder to read. On camera, you often see only faces and shoulders, not full posture or gentle physical contact, like a hand on a knee. Small actions can be misread:

  • A sigh might be seen as criticism
  • Looking away for a moment might be seen as eye rolling
  • Glancing at another screen might be seen as not caring

Stress outside the session can add even more pressure. As the year moves along, many couples feel squeezed by:

  • end-of-year work deadlines and planning
  • School exams and homework stress
  • Financial worries and busy calendars

When people are tired or stretched thin, patience drops. A neutral comment like “Can you explain that again?” might be heard as “You never make sense.” Through a screen, that small misunderstanding can quickly grow if it is not slowed down and checked.

Common Misread Signals in Online Couples Therapy

Certain patterns show up again and again in online couples work. The meaning you give to what your partner does can be very different from what is happening for them inside.

Some common misread signals include:

  • One partner goes quiet. This might be seen as stonewalling or not caring, when they are actually overwhelmed, trying to calm down, or worried they will say something hurtful.
  • A partner looks away or down often. This might be read as boredom, when they are actually trying hard to think, find words, or manage strong feelings.
  • Someone types or looks off camera. This might be seen as checking social media, when they are taking notes or reading something the therapist sent.

Being on camera can also make people feel self-conscious. Some partners worry about how they look, how their voice sounds, or whether they might cry on screen. To protect themselves, they might:

  • Keep a very flat face
  • Speak in a quiet or short way
  • Avoid direct eye contact with the camera

From the other side of the screen, that can look like being distant or not interested, even when they are trying their best.

Even the therapist’s questions can sometimes feel sharp at first. A gentle challenge, such as “What do you think your partner felt in that moment?” might be heard as “You did the wrong thing.” A prompt like “Can we pause and hear the other side?” can sound like taking sides with one partner.

In our work at Michelle Barratt Psychology, we pay close attention to these moments. We slow things down, explain why we are asking certain questions, and make sure both partners know that we are there to support the relationship, not to pick a winner.

Turning Digital Disconnect Into Deeper Understanding

The good news is that online couples therapy can actually help you build clearer, stronger communication, because it invites you to speak about what you see and feel instead of guessing.

Helpful strategies during online sessions include:

  • Naming what you notice: “You look upset to me, is that right?”
  • Checking your understanding: “I heard you say you feel alone when I work late, did I get that?”
  • Owning your story: “I am telling myself that you are annoyed, but I am not sure if that is true.”

These small steps help turn assumptions into questions, which often lowers tension.

Therapists at Michelle Barratt Psychology help couples:

  • Slow down heated conversations so each person can finish their point
  • Unpack loaded words like “always” and “never”
  • Clarify what was meant versus what was heard
  • Notice body cues like tightening in the chest or clenched jaw and use them as signals to pause, rather than push harder

Because non-verbal cues are less clear online, it can also help to agree on simple signals before you start:

  • A hand raised to signal “I need a short pause”
  • A word or phrase that means “I am getting overwhelmed”
  • A gesture for “I would like the therapist to step in here”

These agreed signals give both partners a sense of safety and predictability during difficult topics.

Setting up Your Space to Support Connection Online

The space you choose for online couples therapy matters more than many people expect. A calm, private area can help you feel safer to speak openly and listen fully, especially as homes get busy with school events, visitors, and extra noise.

Some practical tips include:

  • Choose a room with a door that can close, and let others know you are not to be disturbed
  • Place the camera so both partners are comfortably in view, sitting side by side if possible
  • Check your internet, sound, and camera a few minutes before the session
  • Turn off notifications on phones, tablets, and computers
  • Agree that there will be no multitasking, such as emails, housework, or scrolling

A settled space can lower defensiveness. When you are not distracted by pings, background noise, or worries that someone might walk in, it is easier to stay with your feelings, hear your partner’s words, and choose how you want to respond instead of reacting on autopilot.

Choosing Online Support That Helps You Feel Heard

If you and your partner find yourselves stuck in the same arguments, or tiptoeing around topics because they always seem to go wrong, online couples therapy might offer a helpful reset. This can be especially true in late winter and spring, when tiredness and stress have been building for months.

At Michelle Barratt Psychology in Brisbane, our clinicians work with couples to understand the patterns underneath repeated misunderstandings. Together, we explore what each partner is trying to protect, what they hope for, and what they fear. We focus on building emotional safety, so both people can feel heard, even when they strongly disagree.

Online couples therapy is not about perfect communication or never arguing. It is about learning tools you can use between sessions, such as checking your assumptions, explaining your inner world more clearly, and catching misunderstood signals early. With support, many couples find that the same screen that once seemed to create distance can become a place where they practise new ways of listening, speaking, and reconnecting.

Take The Next Step Toward A Stronger Relationship

If you are ready to improve communication and rebuild trust together, our online couples therapy offers a flexible and confidential way to get started. At Michelle Barratt Psychology, we work with you both to understand unhelpful patterns and create practical strategies you can use in everyday life. Reach out to contact us and we will help you find a time and approach that suits you.
